questions.stem: Pr(A) = 0.5, Pr(B) = 0.4 and Pr(A ∩ B) = 0.2. What is Pr(A ∪ B)?
questions.explanation: The addition rule gives Pr(A ∪ B) = Pr(A) + Pr(B) − Pr(A ∩ B) = 0.5 + 0.4 − 0.2 = 0.7. Simply adding to get 0.9 counts the overlap twice.

questions.stem: Events A and B are mutually exclusive. Which statement must be true?
questions.explanation: Mutually exclusive events cannot occur together, so their intersection is empty and has probability 0. The product rule describes independent events, a different idea.

questions.stem: A and B are mutually exclusive, with Pr(A) = 0.3 and Pr(B) = 0.45. What is Pr(A′ ∩ B′)?
questions.explanation: With no overlap, Pr(A ∪ B) = 0.3 + 0.45 = 0.75, and A′ ∩ B′ is the outside of the union, so its probability is 1 − 0.75 = 0.25. Multiplying 0.7 × 0.55 = 0.385 wrongly treats the events as independent.

questions.stem: Pr(A ∪ B) = 0.8, Pr(A) = 0.5 and Pr(B) = 0.6. What is Pr(A ∩ B)?
questions.explanation: Rearrange the addition rule: Pr(A ∩ B) = Pr(A) + Pr(B) − Pr(A ∪ B) = 1.1 − 0.8 = 0.3. The value 0.2 is 1 − 0.8, the probability of neither event.

questions.stem: Pr(A) = 0.6 and Pr(A ∩ B) = 0.25. What is Pr(A ∩ B′)?
questions.explanation: A splits into the part inside B and the part outside it, so Pr(A ∩ B′) = 0.6 − 0.25 = 0.35. The value 0.15 uses Pr(A′) = 0.4 instead of Pr(A).

questions.stem: Pr(A) = 0.45, Pr(B) = 0.35 and Pr(A ∩ B) = 0.15. What is the probability that exactly one of A and B occurs?
questions.explanation: A only is 0.45 − 0.15 = 0.3 and B only is 0.35 − 0.15 = 0.2, so exactly one has probability 0.5. The value 0.65 is Pr(A ∪ B), which also includes the overlap.

questions.stem: In a Venn diagram, Pr(A only) = 0.3, Pr(A ∩ B) = 0.1 and Pr(B only) = 0.4. What is the probability of neither A nor B?
questions.explanation: The four regions of the diagram must add to 1, so Pr(neither) = 1 − (0.3 + 0.1 + 0.4) = 0.2. Leaving the overlap out of the sum gives 0.3.

questions.stem: In a probability table (Karnaugh map) for two events A and B, what do the four inner cells add to?
questions.explanation: The inner cells are A ∩ B, A ∩ B′, A′ ∩ B and A′ ∩ B′, which do not overlap and together cover the whole sample space, so they add to 1. The margins hold the totals Pr(A), Pr(A′), Pr(B) and Pr(B′).

questions.stem: Which formula defines Pr(A | B), for Pr(B) > 0?
questions.explanation: Given that B has occurred, B becomes the reduced sample space, so the probability of A is the share of B that is also in A. Dividing by Pr(A) gives Pr(B | A) instead.

questions.stem: Pr(A ∩ B) = 0.12 and Pr(B) = 0.4. What is Pr(A | B)?
questions.explanation: Pr(A | B) = 0.12/0.4 = 0.3. Multiplying to get 0.048 confuses the definition with the multiplication rule, and 0.2 divides by Pr(B′) = 0.6.

questions.stem: Pr(B) = 0.4 and Pr(A | B) = 0.25. What is Pr(A ∩ B)?
questions.explanation: The multiplication rule gives Pr(A ∩ B) = Pr(A | B) × Pr(B) = 0.25 × 0.4 = 0.1. Dividing 0.25 by 0.4 to get 0.625 runs the definition backwards.

questions.stem: Pr(A) = 0.5, Pr(B) = 0.25 and Pr(A ∩ B) = 0.1. What is Pr(B | A)?
questions.explanation: Given A, divide by Pr(A): Pr(B | A) = 0.1/0.5 = 0.2. The value 0.4 is Pr(A | B) = 0.1/0.25; the two conditional probabilities are generally different.

questions.stem: A fair die is rolled. Given that the result is even, what is the probability that it is greater than 3?
questions.explanation: The reduced sample space is 2, 4, 6, and two of these, 4 and 6, are greater than 3, so the probability is 2/3. The value 1/3 is Pr(even and greater than 3) over the full sample space.

questions.stem: Two fair coins are tossed. Given that at least one shows a head, what is the probability that both show heads?
questions.explanation: Knowing at least one head leaves the reduced sample space HH, HT, TH, and only HH has two heads, so the probability is 1/3. The tempting 1/2 assumes a particular coin is known to be a head.

questions.stem: Two fair dice are rolled. Given that the sum is 8, what is the probability that at least one die shows a 6?
questions.explanation: The outcomes summing to 8 are (2, 6), (3, 5), (4, 4), (5, 3) and (6, 2), and two of these five contain a 6, so the probability is 2/5. The value 11/36 ignores the condition entirely.

questions.stem: A and B are mutually exclusive, with Pr(A) > 0 and Pr(B) > 0. What is Pr(A | B)?
questions.explanation: Pr(A | B) = Pr(A ∩ B)/Pr(B), and the numerator is 0 because A and B cannot occur together. Once B has happened, A is impossible.

questions.stem: Of 200 Year 11 students, 120 study Methods, 80 study Physics and 50 study both. A student who studies Methods is chosen at random. What is the probability they also study Physics?
questions.explanation: The condition restricts attention to the 120 Methods students, of whom 50 study Physics: 50/120 = 5/12. The value 5/8 = 50/80 is the probability of Methods given Physics.

questions.stem: Of 200 Year 11 students, 120 study Methods, 80 study Physics and 50 study both. What is the probability that a student who does not study Physics studies Methods?
questions.explanation: 120 students do not study Physics, and 120 − 50 = 70 of them study Methods, so the probability is 70/120 = 7/12. The value 7/20 divides by all 200 students instead of the reduced sample space.

questions.stem: Pr(A) = 0.6, Pr(B) = 0.5 and Pr(A ∩ B) = 0.35. What is Pr(B | A′)?
questions.explanation: In the probability table, Pr(A′ ∩ B) = 0.5 − 0.35 = 0.15 and Pr(A′) = 0.4, so Pr(B | A′) = 0.15/0.4 = 0.375. The value 0.15 is the joint probability before dividing by Pr(A′).

questions.stem: Events A and B are independent exactly when:
questions.explanation: Independence means one event occurring does not change the probability of the other, which is equivalent to the product rule. Pr(A ∩ B) = 0 describes mutually exclusive events instead.

questions.stem: A and B are independent, with Pr(A) = 0.3 and Pr(B) = 0.5. What is Pr(A ∪ B)?
questions.explanation: Independence gives Pr(A ∩ B) = 0.3 × 0.5 = 0.15, so Pr(A ∪ B) = 0.3 + 0.5 − 0.15 = 0.65. Adding to get 0.8 is only valid for mutually exclusive events.

questions.stem: A and B are independent, with Pr(A) = 0.7 and Pr(B) = 0.5. What is Pr(A | B)?
questions.explanation: For independent events, knowing that B occurred does not change the probability of A, so Pr(A | B) = Pr(A) = 0.7. The value 0.35 is Pr(A ∩ B), before dividing by Pr(B).

questions.stem: A and B are independent, with Pr(A) = 0.2 and Pr(B) = 0.6. What is Pr(A′ ∩ B′)?
questions.explanation: If A and B are independent, so are their complements, so Pr(A′ ∩ B′) = 0.8 × 0.4 = 0.32. The value 0.68 is Pr(A ∪ B), the complement of the answer.

questions.stem: A and B are independent, Pr(A ∪ B) = 0.6 and Pr(A) = 0.2. What is Pr(B)?
questions.explanation: Write p = Pr(B): 0.6 = 0.2 + p − 0.2p, so 0.4 = 0.8p and p = 0.5. The value 0.4 subtracts as though the events were mutually exclusive.

questions.stem: Pr(A) = 0.4, Pr(B) = 0.5 and Pr(A ∪ B) = 0.7. Which statement is true?
options: A and B are neither, as Pr(A ∩ B) = 0.1
A and B are mutually exclusive
A and B are mutually exclusive and independent
questions.explanation: Pr(A ∩ B) = 0.4 + 0.5 − 0.7 = 0.2, which equals 0.4 × 0.5, so the events are independent. They are not mutually exclusive, because their intersection has non-zero probability.

questions.stem: A and B are mutually exclusive, with Pr(A) > 0 and Pr(B) > 0. Which statement is true?
options: Pr(A | B) is equal to Pr(A)
Pr(A ∪ B) is equal to Pr(A) × Pr(B)
A and B cannot be independent
A and B must be independent
questions.explanation: Mutually exclusive means Pr(A ∩ B) = 0, but Pr(A) × Pr(B) is positive, so the product rule fails. Knowing B occurred makes A impossible, which is the opposite of independence.

questions.stem: A basketballer scores each free throw with probability 0.8, independently. What is the probability she scores the first two and misses the third?
questions.explanation: Multiply along one path: 0.8 × 0.8 × 0.2 = 0.128. The value 0.384 counts all three orders of two scores and one miss, which the question does not ask for.

questions.stem: A basketballer scores each free throw with probability 0.8, independently. What is the probability she scores exactly two of three?
questions.explanation: There are three paths with two scores and one miss (SSM, SMS, MSS), each with probability 0.8 × 0.8 × 0.2 = 0.128, so the total is 3 × 0.128 = 0.384. The value 0.512 is the probability of scoring all three.

questions.stem: On a tree diagram, the probabilities on the branches leaving any one point:
options: add to the next stage's probability
questions.explanation: The branches from one point list every possible outcome at that stage, given what happened before, so their probabilities add to 1. Multiplying happens along a path, not across branches.

questions.stem: A bag holds 4 green and 3 yellow counters. Two are drawn without replacement. What is the probability that they are different colours?
questions.explanation: Pr(GY) + Pr(YG) = (4/7)(3/6) + (3/7)(4/6) = 12/42 + 12/42 = 4/7. The value 24/49 uses 7 counters on both draws, which is drawing with replacement, and 2/7 counts only one order.

questions.stem: A bag holds 4 green and 3 yellow counters. Two are drawn without replacement. Given that the second is green, what is the probability that the first was green?
questions.explanation: Pr(both green) = (4/7)(3/6) = 2/7 and Pr(second green) = 2/7 + (3/7)(4/6) = 4/7, so the answer is (2/7)/(4/7) = 1/2. The value 4/7 ignores the information about the second draw.

questions.stem: A box holds 6 good and 4 faulty batteries. Two are chosen at random without replacement. What is the probability that both are faulty?
questions.explanation: (4/10) × (3/9) = 12/90 = 2/15, because after one faulty battery is taken only 3 of the remaining 9 are faulty. The value 4/25 = (4/10)² treats the draws as with replacement.

questions.stem: Which statement is the law of total probability for events A and B?
questions.explanation: A happens either together with B or together with B′, and these cases do not overlap, so Pr(A) = Pr(A ∩ B) + Pr(A ∩ B′), with each term written using the multiplication rule. Adding the two conditional probabilities alone ignores how likely B is.

questions.stem: A factory makes 40% of its parts on machine A, with 5% defective, and 60% on machine B, with 2% defective. What is the probability that a part is defective?
questions.explanation: By the law of total probability, Pr(D) = 0.4 × 0.05 + 0.6 × 0.02 = 0.02 + 0.012 = 0.032. Averaging 5% and 2% to get 0.035 ignores the fact that machine B makes more of the parts.

questions.stem: A factory makes 40% of its parts on machine A, with 5% defective, and 60% on machine B, with 2% defective. A part is defective. What is the probability it came from machine A?
questions.explanation: Pr(A ∩ D) = 0.4 × 0.05 = 0.02 and Pr(D) = 0.032, so Pr(A | D) = 0.02/0.032 = 0.625. The value 0.05 is Pr(D | A), the conditional probability the wrong way round.

questions.stem: If it rains today, the chance of rain tomorrow is 0.6; if not, it is 0.2. The chance of rain today is 0.3. What is the probability of rain tomorrow?
questions.explanation: Pr(rain tomorrow) = 0.3 × 0.6 + 0.7 × 0.2 = 0.18 + 0.14 = 0.32. The value 0.18 counts only the path where it rains today.

questions.stem: If it rains today, the chance of rain tomorrow is 0.6; if not, it is 0.2. The chance of rain today is 0.3. Given rain tomorrow, what is the probability it rained today?
questions.explanation: Pr(rain today ∩ rain tomorrow) = 0.18 and Pr(rain tomorrow) = 0.32, so the answer is 0.18/0.32 = 9/16. The value 0.6 is the conditional probability in the other direction.

questions.stem: A spinner shows 1, 2, 3 or 4 with equal probability and is spun twice. What is the probability that the first number is greater than the second?
questions.explanation: A 4 × 4 grid has 16 outcomes, 4 of which are ties. The other 12 split evenly, so 6 have the first number greater: 6/16 = 3/8. The value 1/2 forgets the ties.

questions.stem: A simulation estimates the probability of drawing two red balls, without replacement, from a bag of 3 red and 5 black. What should each trial do?
options: Toss a coin for each of the two draws and record heads as a red ball
Draw two balls without putting the first back, then return both before the next trial
Draw one ball, put it back, then draw a second ball before the next trial
Draw two balls without replacement and leave both out for all later trials
questions.explanation: Each trial must copy the real experiment, two draws without replacement, and then reset the bag so every trial starts the same. Replacing after the first draw simulates a different experiment, and a coin gives each draw probability 1/2 rather than the bag's 3/8.

questions.stem: A simulation of 100 trials estimates a probability as 0.41, but the theoretical value is 0.4. What is the best explanation?
options: The simulation must have used replacement by mistake
The theoretical value of 0.4 must have been miscalculated
One hundred trials always reproduce the exact value
Simulation estimates vary randomly about the true value
questions.explanation: A simulation gives a relative frequency, which varies from run to run; 41 successes in 100 trials is entirely consistent with a probability of 0.4. More trials would usually bring the estimate closer.
